groups.title: Arriving at the airport
groups.intro: The first forty minutes. Passport control, baggage, a taxi or the train. If you memorise ten of these before boarding in Canada, you land soft.

items.note: Say turismo at passport control even if you're staying longer; it's the default short-stay reason.

items.t: Il mio bagaglio non è arrivato.
items.note: The right form at the airline desk; follow with the baggage-claim ticket.

items.n: Where can I get a taxi?

items.t: Dove si prende il treno per il centro?
items.n: Where do I get the train to the centre?

items.t: Quanto costa il biglietto per Roma Termini?
items.n: How much is the ticket to Roma Termini?
What platform does it leave from?

items.t: Mi scusi, non capisco. Può ripetere, per favore?
items.n: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you repeat, please?

groups.title: Hello and goodbye
groups.intro: Italian greetings change with time of day and formality. In the first weeks: too polite is always better than too casual.

items.n: Hello. (neutral, works all day with strangers)
Good morning (until about 1 p.m., sometimes until the lunch break).
Good evening (from 4-5 p.m. onwards; also used for Good afternoon).
Good night (only when going to bed, not as a leaving greeting).
Goodbye (formal / to someone you may see again).

items.t: A dopo. · A domani. · A presto.
items.n: See you later. · See you tomorrow. · See you soon.

items.t: Bene, grazie. E Lei? · E tu?
items.n: Fine, thank you. And you? (formal · informal)
Nice to meet you. · Pleased to meet you (formal).

groups.title: At the bar · ordering a coffee
groups.intro: The Italian bar is a counter you stand at for 90 seconds. Order, pay at the cassa (sometimes before, sometimes after), tip optional. Il caffè means espresso.

items.n: An espresso with a drop of milk.

items.note: Order cappuccino before 11 a.m. only; after lunch is a mild social crime.

items.t: Uno al cioccolato. · Uno vuoto. · Uno con la marmellata.
items.n: A chocolate one. · A plain one. · A jam one.
At the counter, thanks. (= standing at the bar — cheaper than at a table)
Do I pay before or after?

items.note: By law in Italy since 2022; many places still prefer cash for small amounts.

groups.title: Numbers, time, money
groups.intro: The small vocabulary you'll use every day for prices, times and change.

items.t: Zero, uno, due, tre, quattro, cinque, sei, sette, otto, nove, dieci.
Ha spiccioli? Mi manca il resto.
items.n: Do you have change? I don't have the right change.

items.t: Che ora è? · Che ore sono?
Sono le dieci e un quarto.
A che ora apre il negozio?
items.n: What time does the shop open?

items.t: A che ora chiude la farmacia?
items.n: What time does the pharmacy close?
From 8 to 1, from 4 to 7. (typical shop hours with the lunch break)

groups.title: In town · directions
groups.intro: Everything is five minutes away in an Italian town, until it isn't. Learn to ask with a smile.

items.t: Dove si trova il bar più vicino?

items.n: How do I get to the town hall?
Is it far? · Is it near?
At the traffic light turn left.

items.t: È in fondo a questa via.
items.n: It's at the end of this street.
It's right in front of you.
items.note: What you most hear after wandering.

items.n: Can you mark it on the map?

groups.title: The pharmacy
groups.intro: The pharmacist is the first level of healthcare in Italy. For small problems, go here before you go to the doctor.

items.n: Is it on duty tonight? (pharmacies take turns being open at night)

items.t: Qualcosa per il mal di testa.
Ho la tosse. · Ho la febbre.
items.n: I have a cough. · I have a fever.

items.t: La prendo tre volte al giorno?
items.n: Do I take it three times a day?

groups.title: At the comune · residency
groups.intro: The town hall decides who is officially there. The ufficio anagrafe handles residency; the ufficio stranieri handles the permesso di soggiorno.

items.n: I'd like to register as a resident.

items.t: Ecco il passaporto, il codice fiscale e il contratto di affitto.
items.n: Here are my passport, tax code and rental contract.

items.t: Quando posso venire a ritirare il documento?
items.n: When can I come to collect the document?

items.t: Scusi, non ho capito. Me lo può spiegare più lentamente?
items.n: Sorry, I didn't understand. Can you explain it more slowly?

items.t: Dovrei tornare domani con la marca da bollo?
items.n: Should I come back tomorrow with the revenue stamp?
Is there a form to fill in?

groups.title: Renting a flat
groups.intro: Italian housing has fixed language: inquilino, proprietario, caparra, cedolare secca. Learn the top ten and read the contract before signing.

items.n: I'm looking for a flat to rent.
How much is the rent per month?
Is it a 4+4 contract? (standard long-term residential rental)
Can I register as a resident at this address?

items.t: Devo pagare il bonifico ogni mese?
items.n: Do I pay by bank transfer each month?
I'd like to view the flat, if possible.

items.t: Posso avere il contratto in anticipo?
items.n: Can I have the contract in advance?

groups.title: At the restaurant
groups.intro: Italian meals have a shape: antipasto, primo, secondo + contorno, dolce, caffè, amaro. You order each course when you want it, not all at once.

items.t: Buonasera, un tavolo per due, per favore.
items.n: Good evening, a table for two, please.
We have a reservation for eight.

items.t: Qual è la specialità della casa?

items.n: Is there gluten? I have celiac disease.

items.t: Un bicchiere di vino rosso della casa.
items.n: A glass of house red wine.
A litre of still water. (frizzante = sparkling)

items.note: Il coperto: a small per-person fee (1-3 euros), standard in Italy, usually printed on the menu.

items.t: È tutto buonissimo. Complimenti al cuoco.
items.n: Everything is wonderful. Compliments to the chef.

groups.title: Shopping · food and clothes
groups.intro: The daily shopping language. Fruits by the kilo, clothes by the size, prices by the euro.

items.t: Un chilo di pomodori, per favore.

items.n: Two hundred grams of ham. (un etto = 100 g, standard shopping unit)

items.t: Un panino con prosciutto e mozzarella.
items.n: A sandwich with ham and mozzarella.
I wear a 42. (Italian size for clothes / shoes)
Can I try it on? (m. / f. object)

items.t: Mi sta bene? · Mi sta un po' stretto.
items.n: Does it fit? · It's a bit tight.

items.t: Avete una taglia più grande? · Più piccola?
items.n: Do you have a bigger size? · A smaller one?
I'll take it. · I won't take it.

groups.title: Health · at the doctor
groups.intro: If the pharmacy isn't enough, the medico di base (GP) is the next step. For emergencies: pronto soccorso (ER). Call 112 for all emergencies.

items.t: Vorrei prendere un appuntamento con il dottore.
items.n: I'd like to make an appointment with the doctor.
I'm registered with the local health authority.

items.t: Non sono {{iscritto|iscritta}} alla ASL. È possibile pagare?
items.n: I'm not registered with the ASL. Is it possible to pay?

items.t: Il 112 è il numero d'emergenza unico.

groups.title: Phone, internet, bank
groups.intro: The three services every newcomer sets up in the first fortnight. Carrier, SPID, bank account — in that order.

items.n: I'd like an Italian SIM card.

items.t: Posso tenere il mio numero canadese?
items.n: Can I keep my Canadian number?
I'd like to open a current account.

items.t: Posso avere una carta di debito?
items.n: Can I have a debit card?
I'd like to make a bank transfer.

items.t: Lo SPID è obbligatorio, mi sa.
items.note: SPID (Sistema Pubblico di Identità Digitale) is the login for Italian state websites.

groups.title: When you don't understand
groups.intro: The most useful page of this phrasebook. Nobody expects you to understand everything in your first weeks; everybody expects you to ask.

items.t: Non ho capito. · Non ho capito bene.
items.n: I didn't understand. · I didn't quite understand.
How do you say ___ in Italian?

items.t: Me lo può scrivere, per favore?
items.n: Can you write it down for me, please?

items.note: Formal Lei. In big cities, usually yes; in small towns, often no.

groups.title: Small talk and the social moves
groups.intro: The phrases that make a conversation last three minutes instead of thirty seconds. Learn five, deploy them often.

items.t: Da dove viene? · Da dove vieni?
Vengo dal Canada. · Vengo da Toronto.
items.n: I'm from Canada. · I'm from Toronto.

items.t: Da quanto tempo è in Italia?
items.n: How long have you been in Italy?

items.t: Da due settimane. · Da due anni.
items.n: For two weeks. · For two years.

items.t: Che lavoro fa? · Che lavoro fai?
items.n: What do you do for a living? (formal · informal)

items.t: Mi piace molto l'Italia. · Mi piace la vostra città.
items.n: I like Italy a lot. · I like your city.
Are you here for a long time?
Shall we meet again? Let's swap numbers.

items.t: Prendiamo un caffè una di queste sere?
items.n: Shall we grab a coffee one of these evenings?
See you soon! Enjoy the rest of your day.
